name: Uri
summary: Uri grew from the Reuss valley to a pass state on both sides of the Gotthard, then lost the Leventina in 1798 and kept Urseren.

stops.title: Abbey land under Zähringen rule
text: In 853 King Louis the German gives his lands and rights in Uri to the Fraumünster abbey in Zurich. The abbey owns much of the land.
Outside lords hold the right to judge and protect the valley for the king: the counts of Lenzburg from about 976 to 1173, then the dukes of Zähringen until 1218.
Urseren belongs to the lands of Disentis abbey, on the other side of the Oberalp Pass.

layers.name: Urseren
layers.label: Urseren: land of Disentis abbey

layers.name: Uri
layers.label: Uri: Fraumünster abbey land, dukes of Zähringen as the king's governors (until 1218)

stops.title: Directly under the Empire
text: After 1218 the Habsburgs get rights in Uri. In 1231 King Henry (VII) buys these rights back, and Uri comes directly under the Empire (reichsfrei: no lord between the valley and the king).
In 1239 or 1240 Emperor Frederick II makes Urseren an imperial district and gives it to Count Rudolf of Rapperswil.

layers.name: Urseren
layers.label: Urseren: Disentis abbey land, counts of Rapperswil as imperial governors

layers.name: Uri
layers.label: Uri: directly under the Empire since 1231

stops.title: Uri in the first league
text: Uri is the valley of the Reuss from Lake Uri up to the Schöllenen gorge, with its side valleys. It is one of the first members of the Swiss league, around 1291 or 1309, and surely by 1315.
Urseren, the high valley around Andermatt, is not yet part of Uri.

layers.name: Urseren
layers.label: Urseren: Disentis abbey land, Habsburg as governors since 1283

layers.name: Uri
layers.label: Land of Uri: founding member of the Swiss league

stops.title: Urseren joins Uri
text: In 1410 Uri and Urseren make a Landrecht (a treaty of common citizenship). Urseren keeps its own customs and court, but Uri leads it in war, justice and transit.
Uri now controls the road up to the Gotthard Pass. In 1403 Uri and Obwalden had already moved into the Leventina south of the pass, but they lose it again in 1422.

layers.name: Urseren
layers.label: Urseren: linked to Uri by treaty since 1410, with its own court

layers.name: Uri
layers.label: Land of Uri

stops.title: A pass state across the Gotthard
text: Uri takes the Leventina again in 1439–1441. After the battle of Giornico in 1478 and peace with Milan in 1480, the valley stays with Uri. It is a subject land: Uri sends a bailiff (a governor) to rule it.
From 1503 Uri also rules Bellinzona, the Riviera and the Blenio valley, together with Schwyz and Nidwalden.

layers.name: Leventina
layers.label: Leventina: ruled by Uri alone, about 1441–1798

layers.name: Bellinzona, Riviera, Blenio
layers.label: Bellinzona, Riviera and Blenio: ruled by Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden, 1503–1798

layers.name: Urseren
layers.label: Urseren: linked to Uri by treaty

layers.name: Uri
layers.label: Land of Uri

stops.title: Part of canton Waldstätten
text: In 1798 the Helvetic Republic ends the old order. The Leventina is set free and is no longer ruled by Uri.
Uri becomes two districts, Altdorf and Andermatt, of the new canton of Waldstätten. This canton joins Uri, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden and Zug.

layers.name: Uri
layers.label: Uri: districts Altdorf and Andermatt of canton Waldstätten

layers.name: Rest of Waldstätten
layers.label: Other parts of the Helvetic canton Waldstätten (1798–1801)

layers.name: Leventina
layers.label: Leventina: free of Uri since 1798, later part of Ticino

stops.title: Uri as it is today
text: In 1803 Uri is a canton again. Urseren becomes an equal part of Uri, not a separate valley under a treaty.
Uri tries to get the Leventina back, but it fails. The Leventina stays in the new canton of Ticino. Since then, the borders of Uri have not changed.

layers.name: Uri
layers.label: Canton of Uri, with Urseren (since 1803)

layers.name: Leventina
layers.label: Leventina: part of Ticino since 1803

name: Schwyz
summary: Schwyz added Arth, the March, Einsiedeln, Küssnacht and the Höfe by 1440, shared Gaster and Uznach with Glarus until 1798, gained Gersau in 1817 and was briefly split in 1832–1833.

stops.title: Lenzburg and Einsiedeln
text: Around 1150 the counts of Lenzburg own large estates in the Schwyz valley. The people of Schwyz already argue with Einsiedeln abbey about the border of their pastures. This dispute (the Marchenstreit) goes on for almost 200 years.
Einsiedeln abbey owns the forest land around the monastery and the Höfe on Lake Zurich. The lords of Rapperswil and others hold land in the March.

layers.name: Einsiedeln
layers.label: Einsiedeln abbey and its lands (with the Höfe)

layers.name: March
layers.label: March: lords of Rapperswil and other lords (about)

layers.name: Schwyz
layers.label: Schwyz valley: large estates of the counts of Lenzburg (until 1173)

stops.title: Schwyz becomes reichsfrei
text: The Lenzburg line dies out in 1173. Their lands go to the Kyburgs, the Frohburgs, the lords of Rapperswil and the Habsburgs.
In 1240 Emperor Frederick II puts the valley of Schwyz directly under the Empire, as thanks for its help. The Habsburgs do not accept this, and the conflict goes on.
Küssnacht is ruled by a family of knights who serve the Habsburgs.

layers.name: Einsiedeln
layers.label: Einsiedeln abbey and its lands (with the Höfe)

layers.name: March
layers.label: March: lords of Rapperswil and other lords (about)

layers.name: Küssnacht
layers.label: Küssnacht: knights of Küssnacht, vassals of Habsburg

layers.name: Schwyz
layers.label: Valley of Schwyz: directly under the Empire since 1240

stops.title: Old Land Schwyz
text: The Land of Schwyz is the valley around the village of Schwyz, from Lake Lucerne to the Muota valley and Rothenthurm. It is one of the first members of the Swiss league, around 1291 or 1309, and surely by 1315.
Arth, Küssnacht, Einsiedeln, the March and the Höfe are not yet part of Schwyz.
Einsiedeln abbey still rules its own lands, with the Habsburgs as protectors since 1283. Küssnacht is held by knights who serve the Habsburgs.

layers.name: Arth
layers.label: Arth: joined Schwyz in the 14th century

layers.name: Einsiedeln
layers.label: Einsiedeln abbey and the Höfe (Habsburg protectors since 1283)

layers.name: Küssnacht
layers.label: Küssnacht: knights of Küssnacht, vassals of Habsburg

layers.name: Land Schwyz
layers.label: Old Land of Schwyz: founding member of the Swiss league

stops.title: Schwyz and its outer lands
text: Schwyz grows quickly. It takes Einsiedeln in 1386 and becomes protector (Kastvogt) of the abbey in 1424. It makes treaties with the March from 1386 and holds all of it by 1436. It buys the rights over Küssnacht in 1402. In 1440, after the Old Zurich War, it takes Wollerau and Pfäffikon (the Höfe).

These outer lands belong to Schwyz, but their people have fewer rights than the people of old Schwyz. Together with Glarus, Schwyz also rules Gaster (from 1438) and Uznach (pledged 1437, bought 1469).
Gersau stays a tiny free republic and an ally of the Swiss.

layers.name: Gersau
layers.label: Gersau: small free republic, ally of the Swiss

layers.name: Gaster and Uznach
layers.label: Gaster and Uznach: ruled by Schwyz and Glarus together until 1798

layers.name: Einsiedeln
layers.label: Einsiedeln and abbey lands: under Schwyz since 1386–1424

layers.name: March
layers.label: March: under Schwyz, fully by 1436

layers.name: Höfe
layers.label: Höfe (Wollerau, Pfäffikon): taken by Schwyz in 1440

layers.name: Küssnacht
layers.label: Küssnacht: rights bought by Schwyz in 1402

layers.name: Land Schwyz
layers.label: Land of Schwyz, now with Arth

stops.title: Split between two cantons
text: In 1798 the Helvetic Republic divides the land of Schwyz. Schwyz, Gersau, Küssnacht and Einsiedeln go to the new canton of Waldstätten.
The March and the Höfe go to the canton of Linth, together with Glarus. Gaster and Uznach are no longer ruled by Schwyz.

layers.name: Schwyz in Waldstätten
layers.label: Schwyz, Gersau, Küssnacht, Einsiedeln: part of canton Waldstätten

layers.name: March and Höfe
layers.label: March and Höfe: part of canton Linth (1798–1803)

layers.name: Rest of Waldstätten
layers.label: Other parts of canton Waldstätten

stops.title: Gersau joins for good
text: In 1803 Schwyz is a canton again, with the March, the Höfe, Einsiedeln and Küssnacht. All its people now have equal rights in law.
Gersau and Reichenburg are added in 1803. Gersau becomes part of Schwyz for good in 1817.

layers.name: Gersau
layers.label: Gersau: part of Schwyz for good since 1817

layers.name: Schwyz
layers.label: Canton of Schwyz

stops.title: Outer Schwyz breaks away
text: The outer districts want equal seats in the cantonal council. In 1832 the March, Einsiedeln, Küssnacht and Pfäffikon form their own half-canton, Ausserschwyz (Outer Schwyz).
Old Schwyz, Gersau and Wollerau stay with the old canton.

layers.name: Ausserschwyz
layers.label: Ausserschwyz: breakaway half-canton, 1832–1833

layers.name: Inner Schwyz
layers.label: Canton of Schwyz (inner part), 1832–1833

stops.title: Schwyz reunited
text: In August 1833 federal troops occupy the canton. A new constitution in 1833 joins the two parts again and gives all districts equal rights.
Since then, the borders have not changed. In 1848 Wollerau and Pfäffikon join to form the district of Höfe.

layers.name: Schwyz
layers.label: Canton of Schwyz today

notes: Old Land Schwyz drawn as today's district of Schwyz without Arth; the Iberg and Alpthal area was long disputed with Einsiedeln abbey and is drawn as Schwyz. Reichenburg is drawn with the Einsiedeln abbey lands in 1440. Ausserschwyz is drawn with Freienbach (Pfäffikon) only; Feusisberg is drawn with Wollerau (about). Gaster and Uznach drawn as today's See-Gaster without Rapperswil-Jona. The shared Italian bailiwicks (Bellinzona, Riviera, Blenio) and Gams are not drawn because they do not touch Schwyz.

name: Obwalden
summary: Obwalden, the upper half of Unterwalden, kept the same valley from the Middle Ages and gained the Engelberg valley in 1815.

stops.title: Lenzburg and the new abbey
text: Around 1150 the counts of Lenzburg are strong in Obwalden. They build a castle above Sarnen and give much land to their monastery of Beromünster. Lucerne's monastery (part of Murbach abbey) owns farms in Sarnen, Giswil and Alpnach.
In 1120 a monastery is founded at Engelberg. The abbey becomes the lord of the high valley.

layers.name: Engelberg
layers.label: Engelberg: valley of the abbey (founded 1120)

layers.name: Obwalden
layers.label: Obwalden: counts of Lenzburg with church lands (about; until 1173)

layers.name: Nidwalden
layers.label: Nidwalden: many lords; Lenzburg probably among them (about)

stops.title: Habsburg rule
text: After 1173 the Habsburgs become the strongest lords in Unterwalden. In 1257 they give their lands there as fiefs to local followers.
Around 1247 the people of Sarnen appear for the first time as a valley community. In 1291 the Habsburgs also buy Murbach abbey's rights in Obwalden.

layers.name: Engelberg
layers.label: Engelberg: valley of the abbey

layers.name: Unterwalden
layers.label: Unterwalden: rights held mainly by the counts of Habsburg

stops.title: Unterwalden in the first league
text: Unterwalden has two halves: Obwalden (above the forest) around Sarnen, and Nidwalden (below the forest) around Stans. Unterwalden is one of the first members of the Swiss league, probably soon after 1291 and before 1309.
The Engelberg valley belongs to the abbey of Engelberg. It is a separate small lordship.

layers.name: Engelberg
layers.label: Engelberg: valley of the abbey (Habsburg protectors since 1274)

layers.name: Hergiswil
layers.label: Hergiswil: not yet part of Nidwalden (joined 1378)

layers.name: Obwalden
layers.label: Obwalden: upper half of Unterwalden

layers.name: Nidwalden
layers.label: Nidwalden: lower half of Unterwalden

stops.title: District of canton Waldstätten
text: Obwalden is the first of the old forest cantons to accept the Helvetic constitution, on 1 April 1798.
It becomes the district of Sarnen in the new canton of Waldstätten. Engelberg goes with Nidwalden into the district of Stans.

layers.name: Rest of Waldstätten
layers.label: Other parts of canton Waldstätten, with Engelberg

layers.name: Obwalden
layers.label: Obwalden: district Sarnen of canton Waldstätten

stops.title: Half-canton again
text: In 1803 Obwalden is a half-canton again, as Unterwalden ob dem Wald. The split of Unterwalden into two halves is now official.
Engelberg is given to Nidwalden.

layers.name: Engelberg
layers.label: Engelberg: part of Nidwalden, 1803–1815

layers.name: Obwalden
layers.label: Half-canton Obwalden

stops.title: Engelberg joins Obwalden
text: In 1815 Nidwalden refuses the new Federal Treaty. Federal troops enter Nidwalden, and Engelberg is given to Obwalden.
Engelberg is an exclave (land cut off from the rest of the canton) and becomes Obwalden's seventh commune. Since then, the borders have not changed.

layers.name: Obwalden
layers.label: Canton of Obwalden today, with the Engelberg exclave

notes: Obwalden before 1815 drawn as today's canton without Engelberg. The Leventina (with Uri 1403–1422), Bellinzona (1419–1422) and the Val d'Ossola (1410–1422) were short-lived and are mentioned only here, not drawn.

name: Nidwalden
summary: Nidwalden, the lower half of Unterwalden, added Hergiswil in 1378, held Engelberg from 1798 to 1815 and has kept the same borders since.

stops.title: Many lords and monasteries
text: Around 1150 many nobles and monasteries hold land in Nidwalden, probably also the counts of Lenzburg. Lordship is weak, and local knights often act alone.
In 1120 a monastery is founded at Engelberg. Over time it gets much land in Nidwalden, for example around Buochs.

layers.name: Engelberg
layers.label: Engelberg: valley of the abbey (founded 1120)

layers.name: Nidwalden
layers.label: Nidwalden: many lords; Lenzburg probably among them (about; until 1173)

layers.name: Obwalden
layers.label: Obwalden: counts of Lenzburg with church lands (about)

stops.title: Habsburg, Engelberg and Murbach
text: In the 1200s three lords count most in Nidwalden. The Habsburgs hold the right to judge and protect (Vogtei). Murbach-Lucerne owns a large manor in Stans. Engelberg abbey buys up land from 1260.
In 1274 King Rudolf of Habsburg becomes protector of Engelberg abbey. In 1291 he buys the rights of Murbach-Lucerne.

layers.name: Engelberg
layers.label: Engelberg: valley of the abbey

layers.name: Unterwalden
layers.label: Unterwalden: Vogtei of the counts of Habsburg, with abbey lands

stops.title: Unterwalden in the first league
text: Unterwalden has two halves: Nidwalden (below the forest) around Stans, and Obwalden around Sarnen. Unterwalden is one of the first members of the Swiss league, around 1291 or 1309.
Hergiswil on Lake Lucerne belongs to other lords. The Engelberg valley belongs to its abbey.

layers.name: Engelberg
layers.label: Engelberg: valley of the abbey (Habsburg protectors since 1274)

layers.name: Hergiswil
layers.label: Hergiswil: not yet part of Nidwalden

layers.name: Nidwalden
layers.label: Nidwalden: lower half of Unterwalden

layers.name: Obwalden
layers.label: Obwalden: upper half of Unterwalden

stops.title: Hergiswil joins
text: In 1378 the people of Hergiswil buy the local rights from their lady for 700 guilders. Soon after, Hergiswil joins Nidwalden as its eleventh commune.
From the early 1500s Nidwalden also rules Bellinzona, the Riviera and the Blenio valley, together with Uri and Schwyz, until 1798.

layers.name: Engelberg
layers.label: Engelberg: valley of the abbey (Habsburg protectors since 1274)

layers.name: Nidwalden
layers.label: Nidwalden, with Hergiswil since 1378

layers.name: Obwalden
layers.label: Obwalden: upper half of Unterwalden

stops.title: District Stans with Engelberg
text: In 1798 Nidwalden becomes the district of Stans in the Helvetic canton of Waldstätten. Engelberg is added to this district.
Nidwalden fights against the new order. French troops crush it in September 1798.

layers.name: District Stans
layers.label: District Stans (Nidwalden and Engelberg) of canton Waldstätten

layers.name: Rest of Waldstätten
layers.label: Other parts of canton Waldstätten

stops.title: Half-canton with Engelberg
text: In 1803 Nidwalden is a half-canton again, as Unterwalden nid dem Wald. It keeps Engelberg.

layers.name: Nidwalden
layers.label: Half-canton Nidwalden, with Engelberg (1803–1815)

stops.title: Engelberg is lost
text: In 1815 Nidwalden refuses the new Federal Treaty. Federal troops enter on 18 August. Nidwalden must join, and it loses Engelberg to Obwalden.
Since then, the borders have not changed.

layers.label: Engelberg: part of Obwalden since 1815

layers.label: Canton of Nidwalden today

name: Lucerne
summary: The city of Lucerne joined the Swiss in 1332, built up its rural state from 1380 to 1415, and in 1803 traded Merenschwand for Hitzkirch.

stops.title: Murbach's town and Lenzburg's land
text: The monastery of St. Leodegar in Lucerne belongs to Murbach abbey in Alsace. The town of Lucerne grows next to it, on the abbey's land.
The countryside is part of the Aargau. The counts of Lenzburg are the strongest lords there; they found the monastery of Beromünster. The lords of Wolhusen hold the Entlebuch (about).

layers.name: Lucerne
layers.label: Lucerne: town of Murbach abbey (monastery of St. Leodegar)

layers.name: Entlebuch
layers.label: Entlebuch: lords of Wolhusen (about)

layers.name: Countryside
layers.label: Countryside: counts of Lenzburg and other lords (about; until 1173)

stops.title: Habsburg buys Lucerne
text: The Lenzburg line dies out in about 1172. The Kyburgs and the Habsburgs then compete for the land and found new towns, such as Sursee, Sempach and Richensee.

When the Kyburg main line ends in 1264, the Habsburgs become the main power. In 1291 they buy Murbach's rights over the town of Lucerne. They rule the land from centres such as Sursee, Sempach, Willisau, Wolhusen, Rothenburg and Lucerne.

layers.name: Lucerne
layers.label: Town of Lucerne: bought by Habsburg from Murbach abbey in 1291

layers.name: Countryside
layers.label: Countryside: Habsburg districts and vassals (about)

stops.title: City joins the forest cantons
text: In 1332 the city of Lucerne makes a league with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden. At this time Lucerne rules almost no land outside the town. The countryside around it belongs to the Habsburgs.

layers.name: Lucerne
layers.label: City of Lucerne: member of the Swiss league since 1332

layers.name: Countryside
layers.label: Countryside: Habsburg land (about)

stops.title: A city-state with a large countryside
text: Lucerne begins to buy land in 1380 with Weggis. Its fastest growth comes after the Sempach War (1386–1389), mostly by purchase and pledge: Merenschwand (1394), the Entlebuch (1395 and 1405), Willisau and others.

In 1415 the Habsburgs lose their lands in the Aargau. Their last rights, also over Sursee and the abbey of Beromünster, go to Lucerne. The countryside is a subject land: bailiffs (governors) from the city rule it.
With the other cantons, Lucerne also rules the Freie Ämter (Free Districts), including Hitzkirch. By about 1480 Lucerne's land is mostly complete.

layers.label: Amt Hitzkirch: part of the Freie Ämter, shared with other cantons

layers.label: Merenschwand: ruled by Lucerne, 1394–1798

layers.name: Freie Ämter
layers.label: Freie Ämter: shared with other cantons (from 1415)

layers.name: Lucerne
layers.label: City of Lucerne

layers.name: Lucerne countryside
layers.label: Countryside ruled by the city of Lucerne

stops.title: Hitzkirch in, Merenschwand out
text: In 1798 the old order ends and the countryside gets equal rights. In 1803 Lucerne gets the Amt Hitzkirch from the Helvetic canton of Baden.
In return, Merenschwand goes to the new canton of Aargau. Since then, the borders have not changed.

notes: The 1332 city is drawn as today's municipality of Lucerne (which includes Littau since 2010). The 1415 stop shows the state of about 1415–1480 in one picture; some places came a little later. Amt Hitzkirch drawn as Hitzkirch, Aesch, Ermensee and Schongau (about). The Freie Ämter drawn as today's districts of Muri and Bremgarten (about; the towns of Bremgarten and Mellingen had their own status).

name: Zug
summary: Zug joined the Swiss in 1352 as a town and a rural Amt; the town bought bailiwicks in the west and south, and since 1803 all communes are equal.

stops.title: Loose rule of distant lords
text: Around 1150 the counts of Lenzburg hold loose count rights over the Zug area, but they own little land there. Fraumünster abbey of Zurich has a manor in Cham since at least 858.
Monasteries from outside own much land: Einsiedeln in Ägeri, Kappel and Schänis in Baar, Muri and St. Blasien in the west. Local knights build castles.

layers.name: Cham
layers.label: Cham: manor of Fraumünster abbey, Zurich

layers.name: Zug area
layers.label: Zug area: count rights of Lenzburg (until 1173), many abbey lands

stops.title: Habsburg and Hünenberg
text: After 1240 the counts of Kyburg try to rule Baar and the town of Zug. They may have founded the town. The Kyburg line ends in 1263/1264, and Rudolf of Habsburg takes much of their land.

In 1273 Habsburg gets Zug (about). The town and the outer communities form the Habsburg Amt Zug. In the west, the lords of Hünenberg build their own lordship over Steinhausen, Cham, Hünenberg and Risch.

layers.name: Hünenberg lordship
layers.label: Lords of Hünenberg: Steinhausen, Cham, Hünenberg, Risch

layers.name: Amt Zug
layers.label: Amt Zug: town and outer communities under Habsburg (from about 1273)

stops.title: Town and Amt join
text: In 1352 Zurich besieges Zug. The town and the Amt (the rural communities of Baar, Ägeri and Menzingen) must join the Swiss league.
Habsburg still claims Zug. From 1370 to 1404 Schwyz leads it in practice.

layers.name: Town of Zug
layers.label: Town of Zug: member since 1352

layers.name: Outer Amt
layers.label: Outer Amt: Baar, Ägeri, Menzingen with Neuheim

layers.label: Lords of Hünenberg: Steinhausen, Cham, Hünenberg, Risch (about)

layers.name: Walchwil
layers.label: Walchwil: held by private lords until the town bought it in 1379

stops.title: The town's bailiwicks
text: The town of Zug buys Walchwil in 1379. In the 15th century it buys more land: Cham, Steinhausen, Risch and Oberrüti. Hünenberg comes under the town by a citizenship treaty.
These are bailiwicks (land ruled by a governor) of the town only. The rural Amt stays free and equal to the town.
Zug also shares the rule of the Freie Ämter with other cantons.

layers.label: Freie Ämter: shared with other cantons

layers.name: Outer Amt
layers.label: Outer Amt: Baar, Ägeri, Menzingen with Neuheim

stops.title: District of canton Waldstätten
text: In February 1798 the town gives up its bailiwicks. In May 1798 Zug becomes a district of the new canton of Waldstätten.
From 1799 to 1801 the town of Zug is the capital of Waldstätten.

stops.title: Canton of equal communes
text: In 1803 Zug is a canton again. The old bailiwicks are now equal communes. Oberrüti goes to the new canton of Aargau.
Since then, the borders have not changed.

Hünenberg had a special status (citizenship treaty) but is drawn as a bailiwick. The Freie Ämter drawn as today's districts of Muri and Bremgarten plus the Hitzkirch area (about).

name: Glarus
summary: Glarus joined the Swiss in 1352, ruled Gaster and Uznach with Schwyz and bought Werdenberg in 1517, but lost all its outer lands in 1798–1803.

stops.title: Säckingen abbey's valley
text: In the 700s a noble family gives its land and rights in the Linth valley to the abbey of Säckingen on the Rhine. The abbey stays the main landowner of Glarus for centuries.
In the 1000s and 1100s the counts of Lenzburg protect the abbey's valley and judge for the king. They also hold the high justice in Gaster.

layers.name: Gaster
layers.label: Gaster: high justice of the counts of Lenzburg

layers.name: Glarus
layers.label: Glarus: Säckingen abbey land, counts of Lenzburg as protectors (until 1173)

stops.title: Kyburg as governors
text: After 1173 the king's son Otto of Burgundy holds the right to rule Glarus. After his death in 1200 it goes to the counts of Kyburg.
The Kyburgs also hold the high justice in Gaster.

layers.name: Gaster
layers.label: Gaster: high justice of the counts of Kyburg

layers.name: Glarus
layers.label: Glarus: Säckingen abbey land, counts of Kyburg as governors (1200–1264)

stops.title: Habsburg takes control
text: The Kyburg line ends in 1264. Their rights in Glarus go to Rudolf of Habsburg.
In 1288 the abbess of Säckingen also gives the castles, courts and the office of steward (Meieramt) to King Rudolf's sons. Now Habsburg holds all power in the valley. Gaster is Habsburg land too.

layers.name: Gaster
layers.label: Gaster: Habsburg land

layers.name: Glarus
layers.label: Glarus: Säckingen abbey land under Habsburg rule (1264/1288)

stops.title: Glarus joins the Swiss
text: In 1352 Zurich and the forest cantons make a league with Glarus. At first Glarus is more a protected land than an equal member, and Habsburg soon gets it back.
Glarus beats a Habsburg army at Näfels in 1388. In 1395 it buys the old rights of Säckingen abbey. In 1393 it is named as an equal partner of the league.

layers.name: Glarus
layers.label: Land of Glarus: linked to the Swiss since 1352

layers.name: Gaster
layers.label: Gaster: Habsburg land until 1438

stops.title: Gaster and Uznach with Schwyz
text: During the Old Zurich War, Glarus and Schwyz take Uznach as a pledge in 1437 and Gaster in 1438. Gaster becomes a shared bailiwick of the two cantons. They buy Uznach outright in 1469.
Glarus also takes the whole Kerenzerberg above Lake Walen in 1460.

layers.name: Gaster and Uznach
layers.label: Gaster (from 1438) and Uznach (from 1437/1469): shared with Schwyz

layers.name: Glarus
layers.label: Land of Glarus

stops.title: Werdenberg and Sargans
text: In 1517 Glarus buys the county of Werdenberg in the Rhine valley for 21,500 guilders. It rules Werdenberg alone as a bailiwick until 1798.
Glarus and Schwyz also buy Gams in 1497. From about 1500, Glarus shares the rule of Sargans with six other cantons.

layers.name: Werdenberg
layers.label: Werdenberg: ruled by Glarus alone, 1517–1798

layers.name: Gams
layers.label: Gams: shared with Schwyz since 1497

layers.name: Gaster and Uznach
layers.label: Gaster and Uznach: shared with Schwyz

layers.name: Sargans
layers.label: Sargans: shared with six other cantons

layers.name: Glarus
layers.label: Land of Glarus

stops.title: Canton of Linth
text: In spring 1798 the old cantons set their bailiwicks free. In May 1798 the French join Glarus with its old subject lands and nearby areas into the canton of Linth. Its capital is the town of Glarus.

layers.name: Glarus
layers.label: Glarus: part of the Helvetic canton Linth

layers.name: Rest of Linth
layers.label: Other parts of canton Linth (1798–1803)

stops.title: Glarus alone
text: In 1803 Glarus is a canton again, but without its old subject lands. Werdenberg, Sargans, Gaster and Uznach go to the new canton of St. Gallen.
Since then, the outer borders have not changed. In 2011 the 25 communes merge into three.

layers.name: To St. Gallen
layers.label: Former Glarus lands: part of St. Gallen since 1803

layers.name: Glarus
layers.label: Canton of Glarus today

notes: Glarus is drawn as today's whole canton from 1352, because today's commune of Glarus Nord cannot be split; Bilten, Niederurnen, Oberurnen and Filzbach came in the early 1400s and the Kerenzerberg in 1460. Werdenberg drawn as Buchs, Grabs and Sevelen; Wartau is drawn with Sargans. Gaster and Uznach drawn as today's See-Gaster without Rapperswil-Jona. Canton Linth drawn only roughly (Werdenberg, Sargans, See-Gaster, March, Höfe).
